stories.title: Nvidia Backstops the Largest Data Center Ever Built
stories.story:
On a decommissioned uranium-enrichment site roughly fifty miles south of Columbus, the most expensive construction project in computing history is taking shape — and the financing structure holding it together may matter as much as the concrete.

Nvidia is in advanced talks to guarantee $250 billion in lease and construction financing so that OpenAI can occupy a 10-gigawatt data center campus being developed by SoftBank's energy subsidiary, SB Energy. In a parallel negotiation, Nvidia is also discussing funding OpenAI's chip purchases for the site, a figure that could reach $350 billion. Combined, the two commitments would approach the entire annual GDP of a mid-sized European economy.

The mechanism behind the deal reveals the circular logic now running through AI finance. OpenAI cannot obtain investment-grade credit on its own — it remains unprofitable despite a valuation near $1 trillion — so it needs Nvidia's balance sheet to reassure lenders. Nvidia, in turn, is essentially pre-selling demand for its own chips years into the future, guaranteeing a customer to justify the guarantee. SoftBank carries more than $130 billion of debt funding buildouts across three continents, and the power for the Ohio campus is underwritten by $33 billion Japan committed under a recent U.S. trade deal. The Commerce Secretary controls which companies receive access to that power.

The first 800-megawatt phase is scheduled for 2028. If completed, it would give OpenAI its first owned infrastructure, ending dependence on Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle. The risk is also new: if AI revenue doesn't scale to match these obligations, the circular chain of guarantees unwinds in every direction at once.
stories.hook: The chip company is guaranteeing the loans to build the building that will buy its chips — and somehow that's the stable version of the plan.

stories.title: An AI Cracked Encryption Problems That Stumped Experts for Years
stories.story:
The way cryptographic algorithms get tested has barely changed in decades: publish the design, invite the world's sharpest mathematicians to attack it, and if no one breaks it after years of review, call it safe. That process, painstaking and slow, is one of the few quality controls standing between private data and chaos.

On July 28, Anthropic disclosed that its unreleased Claude Mythos Preview model had punched a hole in that tradition. Working largely autonomously over roughly 60 hours, the model found an improved attack on HAWK — a post-quantum digital signature scheme that NIST advanced to the third round of its standardization process in May, and the last lattice-based candidate still standing. Human experts had reviewed HAWK for two years without finding this flaw. Mythos located a symmetry buried in the algorithm's lattice structure that no reviewer had thought to exploit, effectively cutting HAWK's smallest key strength in half.

The model also invented a technique it called a Möbius Bridge while attacking a reduced-round version of AES, the cipher that encrypts most of the world's internet traffic, making the best-known attack 200 to 800 times faster. A follow-up result broke 13 rounds of LEA — a Korean and ISO lightweight encryption standard used in phones and IoT devices — in under an hour on a desktop.

Anthropics says none of these results threaten production systems today. HAWK is not yet deployed; the AES finding targets a research variant, not the full cipher. But the structural shift is profound. AI has moved from finding implementation bugs in cryptographic code to finding algorithmic flaws in the mathematics itself — the kind of work that previously required years of human specialization. The cost for each discovery: roughly $100,000 in compute. That is cheap enough to run routinely, which means the window in which a nation-state or well-funded adversary could use similar tools offensively before defenders catch up is a question worth taking seriously.
stories.hook: For thirty years we tested encryption by having the best mathematicians try to break it — and it turns out we can now outsource that to a model and get the answer in 60 hours.
stories.source: Anthropic Research / The Next Web / The Hacker News

stories.title: The Fed Holds, but Kevin Warsh Has Changed the Rules
stories.story:
Today the Federal Reserve announced its interest rate decision at 2:00 p.m. ET — and almost nobody expected a surprise. Markets had priced in a hold, keeping the federal funds rate at its target range of 3.50% to 3.75%, where it has sat since December 2025. That would mark five consecutive meetings without a move, a stretch of paralysis unusual for a central bank facing inflation running at 4.2% annually — the highest in three years.

But the story is not the number. It is the man delivering it. Kevin Warsh, who replaced Jerome Powell as Fed Chair earlier this year, has quietly dismantled one of the Fed's most powerful tools: forward guidance. Where Powell spent years carefully telegraphing future moves so that markets could price them in gradually, Warsh has declared the Fed will say less — and mean it. No dot plot accompanies today's meeting. No updated economic projections. Just a shortened statement and a press conference that experts expect to reveal little.

This is a philosophical revolution dressed as bureaucratic housekeeping. Forward guidance became central bank orthodoxy after the 2008 financial crisis, when rates were pinned at zero and the Fed needed language to do what rates could not. Warsh has long argued that this practice distorted markets and made the Fed hostage to its own words. Pure data dependence, he says, is the corrective.

The practical consequence is that markets are flying partially blind. With oil prices surging again on renewed Middle East fighting — American crude jumped roughly 5% overnight — and the June dot plot showing half the committee already penciling in a hike by year-end, investors face a Fed that is both more hawkish in posture and more opaque in communication. September is now the meeting everyone is watching, and Warsh will give them almost nothing to go on until then.
stories.hook: The Fed used to promise you a map; now it just hands you a compass and wishes you luck.
stories.source: Cambridge Currencies / CNBC / CBS News / Motley Fool

stories.title: Meta Bets $135 Billion on AI Before Proving It Pays
stories.story:
For the past decade, Meta's business model was elegantly simple: show ads to billions of people, keep costs lean, print cash. Today, after the market close, that model faces its most consequential stress test. Meta reports Q2 2026 earnings with Wall Street expecting roughly $60 billion in revenue — near the top of the company's own guidance — and earnings per share essentially flat year-over-year despite revenue growing close to 27%. That gap between the top line and the bottom line is the real story.

The cause is not a mystery. Meta raised its full-year capital expenditure forecast to between $125 billion and $145 billion — roughly the annual GDP of Hungary — to fund data centers, AI chips, and computing capacity. For context, that is more than double what the company spent as recently as two years ago. Free cash flow, once Meta's most celebrated metric, has begun to compress sharply under the weight of it.

What makes today's report structurally important is that Meta currently has no cloud business — no AWS, no Azure — through which to monetize the infrastructure it is building. Every other hyperscaler spending at this scale can point to a revenue line that justifies the investment. Meta cannot, yet. Negotiations with Anthropic over a potential compute partnership have been reported but nothing is confirmed, and analysts note that any concrete update on that front during today's earnings call would be the first real evidence that Zuckerberg's pivot has a commercial architecture behind it, not just a vision.

The deeper question is whether AI is actually improving the advertising engine enough to fund the transition. In Q1, ad impressions rose 19% and the average price per ad climbed 12% — strong numbers. But if capex keeps rising faster than those gains compound, the arithmetic eventually turns hostile. Investors have already expressed unease: the stock has shed nearly 10% year-to-date heading into today's print. The market is not asking whether Meta is growing. It is asking whether Meta knows what it is becoming.
stories.hook: Meta is spending like a cloud company but still earning like an ad company — and today is when it has to explain the gap.
stories.source: Meta Investor Relations; Motley Fool; indmoney.com Q2 2026 earnings preview

stories.title: Oil Whipsaws Markets as Iran Attack Upends Fed Day
stories.story:
For roughly three days, the oil market exhaled. Brent crude posted its biggest three-day decline since April 2020 after Iran signaled it would pause strikes as long as Washington did the same. Traders unwound their risk premiums and equity futures climbed. Then, overnight into July 29, the US military reported it had intercepted an Iranian "attempted surprise attack" on American troops. Within hours, West Texas Intermediate crude jumped roughly 5% back above $83 a barrel, equity-index futures turned negative, and Treasury futures slipped.

The timing is almost cruelly precise. Today is the final day of the Federal Reserve's July meeting — the moment Chair Kevin Warsh announces whether rates stay, rise, or signal something worse. Crude is up nearly 20% for the month of July alone, which means headline inflation data for August will almost certainly read hotter than June's relatively cool 3.5% print. That gives hawks on the FOMC — reportedly including Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan and Cleveland's Beth Hammack — live ammunition for a dissent or an outright push to hike. Bond markets had already priced better than a one-in-three chance of a rate increase even before this morning's flare-up.

The mechanism is straightforward but underappreciated: oil is not merely an energy input. It is the inflation variable most visible to ordinary consumers — at the gas pump, in shipping costs, in airfares — and therefore the one most likely to reshape expectations. Warsh, who has declared he has "no tolerance" for elevated prices, now faces a press conference where every answer about the future path of rates will be shadowed by a barrel price that moved 5% while he was sleeping. A hawkish hold is the consensus bet, but in a conflict with no clear off-ramp, September is very much alive.
stories.hook: The Fed doesn't set oil prices, but oil prices increasingly set the Fed.
stories.source: Bloomberg, Saxo Bank Market Quick Take, Yahoo Finance Markets
